title: Lesson 34: Integration: where AI plugs into your existing systems
description: Grounded in Lesson 34 of the AI Adoption series: the six integration terms (integration surface, connector, API, retrieval, read versus write scope, source of truth), the five-rung integration ladder, the five-question gate plus the prompt-injection question for acting systems, the nine-column connection inventory, five failure modes the inventory will not catch, and the reversibility-first order of work.

questions.question: A connector is built on one shared service credential so the pilot can start faster. What problem does that design create?
options: The assistant answers slowly, because every request is re-authorized against the same account
Usage reporting becomes unreliable, because all questions arrive under one identity
The assistant can reach records that the person asking is not allowed to open
The connection fails whenever the credential owner is unavailable or changes roles
questions.explanation: A shared credential carries whatever access the account holds rather than the access of the person asking, so the assistant can surface records a user cannot open. Mirroring each user's permissions is the safer default, and a connection that cannot refuse a request is not ready.

questions.question: A team wants to move a use case from reading curated documents to writing records in a system of record within a month. What does the integration ladder require?
options: The move is allowed once the vendor confirms that the write path is supported and documented
One rung per quarter, and only after the use case shows value at the rung it occupies
The climb is allowed if the writing step is limited to internal records rather than customer ones
The two rungs may be combined when the same team owns both of the connected systems
questions.explanation: Integration is a ladder, and each rung multiplies both the value and the blast radius, so a use case earns the next rung by demonstrating value at the one it holds. Climbing two rungs in a single push is how a pilot becomes an incident.

questions.question: Three candidate connections compete for one quarter of engineering time. How should they be ordered?
options: By announced business value, largest first, so the program can show results early
By the size of the team that requested each one, so the loudest need goes first
By reversibility of the worst likely failure first, then by the population that benefits
By technical difficulty, easiest first, so that the team builds confidence before harder work
questions.explanation: Rank by how easily the worst likely failure can be undone: read-only connections to curated content go first, and writes to anything leaving the company go last. Then weigh how many people benefit and whether the connection removes a step rather than adding one.
